parsed.wine_summary: The High Trellis Cabernet is d'Arenberg's statement wine from McLaren Vale, one of Australia's most consistent warm-climate regions. d'Arenberg has built its reputation on detailed terroir work in McLaren Vale since 1912, and this bottling shows why—it's a Cabernet that sits between the ripe, fruit-forward style of warm Australia and the structural intensity you'd expect from cooler zones. The wine doesn't apologize for its warmth, but it doesn't surrender to it either. Terra rossa soils (iron-rich clay over limestone) are the key: they retain water through hot summers and force the vine to struggle slightly, which concentrates flavor and builds tannin complexity that keeps the wine from feeling one-dimensional.
parsed.terroir_expression: McLaren Vale's terra rossa and rendzina soils over limestone bedrock sit between 50–350 meters elevation, with the coolest sites toward the Mount Lofty Ranges foothills to the east and warmer blocks closer to the Gulf St Vincent coast. The High Trellis vineyard occupies the warmer western side, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 30°C and the limestone subsoil reflects heat back into the canopy. This drives ripe blackcurrant and dark cherry flavors, but the shallow, iron-rich topsoil limits vigor—vines can't just gorge on water and nitrogen. The result is concentrated fruit with firm tannins and a mineral spine from the limestone. You taste this as cassis-forward aromatics with a slight graphite edge and tannins that grip the palate without softening into velvet.
parsed.vinification_summary: d'Arenberg uses traditional methods: hand-harvested fruit, natural fermentation with wild yeast, and extended maceration (prolonged skin contact) to extract tannins and color from Cabernet's thick skins. The wine likely sees oak aging (French or American; d'Arenberg uses both depending on the wine), which adds cedar and vanilla notes without masking the fruit. Extended maceration is crucial here—it's the reason the wine has structure and grip despite the warm climate; without it, warm-region Cabernet can taste soft and one-note. The 14.2–14.5% ABV across vintages shows restraint for the region; d'Arenberg picks at physiological ripeness rather than maximum sugar, preserving acidity and preventing the wine from tasting hot or overripe.

parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm, gripping tannins and dark cherry-cassis fruit anchored by mineral limestone notes
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2020 and 2013 vintages now through 2030; the wine is accessible young but will develop secondary complexity (tobacco, leather, dried plum) over 5–7 years. Store upright in cool conditions; McLaren Vale Cabernet doesn't require decades of cellaring to show well.
parsed.value_assessment: $25–35 USD for current vintages (2020, 2013). Direct competitors include Wynns Coonawarra Cabernet and mid-tier Barossa offerings at the same price. The High Trellis is worth the money because it has the structure and complexity of wines $10–15 more expensive; most warm-climate Australian Cabernets at this price are softer and less interesting. d'Arenberg's reputation and consistent quality seal it.
parsed.market_position: This wine appears on serious wine lists in Australia and the US (especially restaurants with Australian focus), but it's equally at home in retail shops targeting wine-curious drinkers who want something beyond supermarket Cabernet. d'Arenberg's cult following in Australia means the wine moves fast domestically; international availability is solid but not ubiquitous. It's a wine for people who've moved past brand-name Australian Shiraz and want to explore regional Cabernet.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this if you want soft, fruit-forward Australian red—it's not that wine. The High Trellis is built on tannin and mineral structure, which means it needs food or time in the cellar to show its best. Buy it if you like Coonawarra Cabernet or cool-climate Bordeaux but want something with more ripe fruit and less herbaceousness; it's the bridge between those worlds. The 2013 vintage is drinking beautifully now and will age another 5–7 years; 2020 is tighter and will benefit from 2–3 years of bottle age.
